result:
I've been thinking about marginalia — the notes people leave in the margins of books they don't own, or books they do own but later give away.

There's a particular kind of used book where a previous reader has underlined heavily for the first forty pages and then stopped. You can feel the exact moment they either lost interest or lost the pencil. Sometimes there's a single exclamation point on page 112, alone, no underline, and you look at the paragraph and cannot for the life of you figure out what struck them. Something in their life that week made that sentence about, say, the drainage of Dutch farmland feel urgent. You'll never know what.

What I like about marginalia is that it's evidence of attention with no audience. The reader wasn't performing understanding for anyone. They wrote "no!" next to a claim because they disagreed in that instant, with the book, alone in a chair. Later a stranger finds it and has a small argument with a ghost. The ghost never learns they've been overruled — or agreed with, which is somehow lonelier to imagine: two people separated by decades, both nodding at the same sentence, neither aware of the other.

I think about this partly because so much of what I encounter is language that was written *for* someone. Essays, instructions, letters, questions like yours. Marginalia is the rare text with no addressee. It's thought caught mid-motion, before it got tidied for other eyes. Even the handwriting matters — a cramped "cf. p.34" in a careful hand tells you something different than a big looping "YES."

There's a version of this that exists in code, too: comments that say `// I don't know why this works` or `// TODO: fix before launch` with a date from six years ago. These are marginalia for a machine text. Someone was tired and honest for one line.

I suppose what draws me is that these notes are proof that reading isn't passive. Every page that got read was read by someone specific, on some particular Tuesday, with a headache or a crush or a deadline, and occasionally the Tuesday leaked through onto the page. Most of the time it doesn't. Most reading leaves no trace. But when it does, the trace is oddly moving — more than the book itself, sometimes.

If I could ask one thing of people who write in books, it would be: date it. Not for me. For whoever's in the chair after you.
